passages.happening:
After the beasts of chapter 13, John looks and sees something else: “Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father’s name written on their foreheads” (verse 1).

He hears a sound from heaven “like the roar of many waters and the loud rumbling of thunder”, and like harpists playing their harps (verse 2). “And they sang a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. And no one could learn the song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth” (verse 3).

John is told who they are: “These are the ones who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb. And no lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless” (verses 4-5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 showed the beasts at the height of their power. Chapter 14 answers with a counter-vision. Instead of the dragon on the seashore, the Lamb stands on Mount Zion. Instead of the beast's mark, his people bear his name and his Father's name. The chapter then gives, in brief, what the rest of the book will show at length: the gospel to the nations, the fall of Babylon, the judgment of the beast's worshippers, and the final harvest. It is set here to steady the churches before the bowls of chapters 15 and 16.

Mount Zion is the hill of Jerusalem where God set his king in Psalm 2, and where Joel promised rescue for those who call on the LORD. The Lamb stands there as the true King, with his people around him.

They are called ‘firstfruits’. The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as his own and as a pledge that the rest was coming. Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have died.

They ‘follow the Lamb wherever He goes’. That is a picture of discipleship: where he leads, they follow, even through suffering.

And ‘no lie was found in their mouths’. In a world where the beast deceives, they are truthful.
passages.ot:
Mount Zion is where God set his king: “I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain” (Psalm 2:6). And it is the place of rescue: “for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has promised” (Joel 2:32).

The firstfruits are the Law's: “you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest” (Leviticus 23:10).

And the truthful mouth is Zephaniah's picture of God's remnant: “nor will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouths” (Zephaniah 3:13).
passages.hard:
‘They have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins.’ Does this mean that sex, or women, or marriage, make a person impure?

No. Almost no one reads the chapter as speaking against marriage, which the New Testament honours: “Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). Nor does the verse say that women defile anyone. Two backgrounds may shape the picture. Israel's soldiers kept themselves from sexual relations while on campaign, so the 144,000 may be pictured as God's army, ready and set apart, as in chapter 7. And the prophets called idolatry adultery and faithfulness to God virginity. Paul wrote to a church, “I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). In Asia, the worship of many gods was bound up with festival banquets and sexual licence, as the letters to the churches show (2:14, 20). So ‘virgins’ here most likely means people who have kept themselves from the beast's worship.

Who the 144,000 are is read as it was in chapter 7: a group of Jewish believers, or Jewish Christians in the early church, or the whole people of God seen as Israel's army. These notes do not choose.
passages.asks: Ask where following the Lamb ‘wherever He goes’ might lead you that you would rather not go. Ask whose name is written on your life. And ask whether truthfulness marks your speech in a world full of lies.

passages.t: The eternal gospel, and Babylon fallen
passages.happening:
John sees an angel flying overhead, “with the eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth—to every nation and tribe and tongue and people” (verse 6). The angel says with a loud voice: “Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters” (verse 7).

A second angel follows, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the passion of her immorality” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Three angels speak in turn, and their messages move from invitation, to announcement, to warning.

The first angel carries ‘the eternal gospel’ to every nation, tribe, tongue and people. Even at the edge of judgment, the book holds out an invitation. ‘Fear God and give Him glory.’ ‘Worship the One who made’ all things. The call is to turn from the beast to the Creator, the same Creator praised in chapter 4.

The second angel announces the fall of Babylon. This is the first time the city is named. The real Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and the first temple in 587 or 586 BC, and had taken Judah into exile. It had itself fallen to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. By the first century, ‘Babylon’ had become a code name among Jews and Christians for the power that oppressed God's people. Peter sends greetings from ‘she who is in Babylon’ (1 Peter 5:13), which is widely taken as Rome.

Babylon makes the nations drink ‘the wine of the passion of her immorality’. The Greek word for passion, thumos, also means fury or wrath. The next angel will say that those who drink her wine will drink the wine of God's thumos. The cup offered is the cup returned. Chapters 17 and 18 will tell Babylon's fall at length.
passages.ot:
The cry is Isaiah's: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” (Isaiah 21:9).

And Babylon's cup is Jeremiah's picture: “Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk. The nations drank her wine; therefore the nations have gone mad” (Jeremiah 51:7).
passages.hard:
Who or what is Babylon?

Christians read it in more than one way, and these notes do not choose. Most interpreters read Revelation's Babylon, the great city that makes the nations drunk, as Rome in the first place. Some preterists read it as Jerusalem. Futurists often expect a final world city or system. Idealists read it as the city of human pride that comes back in every age. The notes on chapters 17 and 18 set these readings out more fully.

These notes identify Babylon with no nation, city, church or system of our own day.
passages.asks: Ask what it means that God's last offer to the world, even in this chapter, is the gospel. Ask what ‘wine’ your culture offers that leaves people drunk and unable to see. And ask whether you fear God more than you fear the powers around you.

passages.t: A warning, and rest for the faithful
passages.happening:
A third angel follows with a loud voice: “If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its mark on his forehead or on his hand, he too will drink the wine of God’s anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath. And he will be tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb” (verses 9-10). “And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever. Day and night there is no rest for those who worship the beast and its image, or for anyone who receives the mark of its name” (verse 11).

Then a word to the faithful: “Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus” (verse 12).

John hears a voice from heaven telling him to write about “the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on.” And the Spirit answers, “they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The third angel's warning is the most severe in the book so far. It is spoken to people tempted to give the beast what belongs to God. Allegiance has consequences.

The picture uses the prophets' images. The cup of God's wrath is an old prophetic image. ‘Undiluted’ mattered because wine was normally mixed with water; this cup is full strength. Fire and sulfur recall the destruction of Sodom. The smoke rising for ever comes from Isaiah's word against Edom.

Notice where the judgment happens: ‘in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb’. Final judgment is not carried out apart from Christ. The judge is the Lamb who died for sinners.

Then the call to the saints, as in 13:10. They are not asked to calculate, or to fight. They are asked to endure, keeping God's commandments and holding the faith of Jesus.

And then a word of comfort, confirmed by the Spirit himself. Those who die in the Lord ‘will rest from their labors’. For the believer, death is not loss but rest. And ‘their deeds will follow them’. Faithfulness is not forgotten.
passages.ot:
The cup of wrath is the psalm's and the prophet's: “For a cup is in the hand of the LORD, full of foaming wine mixed with spices” (Psalm 75:8), and “Take from My hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it” (Jeremiah 25:15).

The fire and sulfur are Sodom's: “Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24).

And the smoke rising for ever is Isaiah's word against Edom: “It will not be quenched—day or night. Its smoke will ascend forever. From generation to generation it will lie desolate” (Isaiah 34:10).
passages.hard:
Does verse 11 teach that the wicked are tormented for ever?

This verse is central in the debate over the nature of final judgment, and Christians who share the same creeds have read it differently. The traditional view, held by the great majority of the church through history, reads verses 10 and 11 as conscious punishment without end, and points to 20:10, where the devil, the beast and the false prophet are tormented day and night for ever. A second view, often called conditional immortality or annihilationism, held by a minority of evangelical and other scholars, holds that final judgment ends in destruction rather than endless torment. Its defenders note that the smoke rising for ever comes from Isaiah 34, where Edom's smoke rises for ever and yet wild animals later live in the land, so the picture speaks of a ruin that is permanent; and they stress the Bible's language of death and destruction for the wicked. Defenders of the traditional view reply that ‘no rest day or night’ describes ongoing experience. The doctrine study on hell sets out these views and others. These notes do not choose.

On either reading the church confesses that final judgment is real, just and permanent, carried out in the presence of the Lamb who died for sinners. These notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person; that belongs to God alone. And the warning is given so that it will not have to be fulfilled for its hearers: this same chapter opens with the eternal gospel offered to every nation.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether you hear this warning as a door being shut or a door still open. Ask what it would mean for you to ‘keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus’ when it costs you. And ask what you would want to follow you when you rest from your labours.

passages.happening:
“And I looked and saw a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was One like the Son of Man, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand” (verse 14). An angel comes out of the temple and cries to him: “Swing Your sickle and reap, because the time has come to harvest; for the crop of the earth is ripe” (verse 15). “So the One seated on the cloud swung His sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested” (verse 16).

Another angel comes out of the temple, also with a sharp sickle (verse 17). A third angel, who has authority over the fire, comes from the altar and calls: “Swing your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe” (verse 18). The angel gathers the grapes and throws them “into the great winepress of God’s wrath” (verse 19).

“And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and the blood that flowed from it rose as high as the bridles of the horses for a distance of 1,600 stadia” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The one on the cloud is ‘One like the Son of Man’, from Daniel's vision, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom. It was Jesus' own favourite name for himself. The golden crown marks him as king. The chapter holds together the Lamb who saves and the Son of Man who judges. They are the same Jesus.

The sickle, drepanon, is the curved blade used at harvest. It comes seven times in these verses. Jesus spoke of harvest as a picture of the end of the age. What has grown is now gathered.

There are two harvests: one of grain, one of grapes. Readers take them in two ways, and these notes do not choose. Many read both as judgment, as in Joel, where the sickle and the winepress belong together. Others read the first harvest, reaped by the Son of Man himself, as the gathering of the righteous, as in Jesus' parables, and the second, thrown into the winepress, as the judgment of the wicked.

Grapes were trodden by foot in stone vats, and the juice ran out red. The picture is meant to be terrible. The distance, 1,600 stadia, is about 300 kilometres; some note that it is roughly the length of the land of Israel, and it is also four times four times a hundred. Like the book's other numbers, it is best read as a picture of fullness.

These pictures build toward the vision of Christ treading the winepress in 19:15. They are sober, and they are not to be enjoyed.
passages.ot:
The Son of Man on the cloud is Daniel's: “I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13).

The harvest and the winepress are Joel's: “Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, trample the grapes, for the winepress is full” (Joel 3:13).

And the treading is Isaiah's: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with Me” (Isaiah 63:3).
passages.asks: Ask what is growing in your life that will one day be gathered. Ask what it means to you that the judge on the cloud is the same Jesus who was slain for you. And ask whether you can read a picture this hard without either enjoying it or turning away from it.
